paragraphs: Rahva of Pumbedita transmits in Rav Yehudah’s name. Heilprin quotes Berakhot 18a as ‘Rahva said that R' Yehudah said: Anyone who sees a dead person and does not accompany him,’ etc. The checked Bavli reads Rav Yehudah. Shabbat 63, beginning of a: ‘Rahva said that R' Yehudah said: Jerusalem's wood was cinnamon.’ Heilprin quotes Menahot 33b as ‘Rahva said that R' Yehudah said: Bei Harzikei requires two mezuzot.’ The checked Bavli reads Rav Yehudah. Rashi and Tosafot explain nothing about why he called him R' Yehudah rather than Rav Yehudah. Pesahim 13, beginning of b: ‘Rahva said that R' Yehudah said: the Temple Mount had a double stoa.’ Tosafot write: he said R' Yehudah because Rav Yehudah was his principal teacher, so he called him ‘Rabbi.’ End quotation. Rashi explains the double stoa and leaves the title unexplained. Sukkah 45, beginning of a: ‘Rahva said that Rav Yehudah said’—it should read R' Yehudah—‘the Temple Mount had a double stoa.’ Pesahim 52b: Rav Safra said, ‘Hold onto this rule of Rav Huna, who precisely learned teachings from his teacher's mouth, like Rahva of Pumbedita’—who took care with his teaching to know from whom he received it, Rashi explains—‘for Rahva said that R' Yehudah said.’ The checked Bavli has Rav Yehudah, while Rashi’s lemma has R' Yehudah. Rashi: he was uncertain whether he heard it from Rav Yehudah or R' Yehudah Nesia, who was also in that generation. One cannot say that he certainly heard R' Yehudah Nesia and therefore said R' Yehudah, for then he should have said R' Yehudah Nesia. Necessarily his unqualified R' Yehudah reflects uncertainty. Berakhot 33b: R' Zeira said, ‘Hold onto R' Hiyya bar Abba, who precisely learned teachings from the master's own mouth, like Rahva of Pumbedita, for Rahva said that R' Yehudah said: the Temple Mount had a double stoa.’ Rashi explains: he was precise about his teacher's language, saying stoa although the Mishnah calls it an itztabba in Pesahim and Sukkah. He kept his teacher's language and did not say ‘it had a double itztabba.’ Some explain Rahva's precision from ‘R' Yehudah’: he preserved uncertainty about the authorities, whether R' Yehudah or Rav Yehudah. But I have great difficulties: first, Rahva never saw R' Yehudah—neither R' Yehudah bar Ilai nor R' Yehudah Nesia. Moreover, all amoraim also take care to attribute a matter to its speaker. Moreover, one cannot say from this that he was precise about the teaching's wording, only about uncertainty regarding the authorities. End quotation.

On Rashi’s statement that Rahva did not see R' Yehudah Nesia, Maharshal proposes reading R' Yehudah Ha-Nasi. One must then also emend Beitzah, which I shall copy shortly, and Pesahim 52b, quoted above, where Rashi likewise has uncertainty between Rav Yehudah and R' Yehudah Nesia. I wished to suggest that Maharshal intended to emend to ‘Rahva did not see R' Yehudah Ha-Nasi,’ rather than R' Yehudah Nesia. For Bava Kamma 19b says that R' Yehudah Nesia and R' Hoshaya sat at R' Yehudah’s entrance and a question arose between them. Heilprin proposes reading ‘Rav Yehudah’ and cites Yuhasin under Hoshaya. Yuhasin asks how R' Yehudah Nesia came to be at Rav Yehudah’s entrance in Babylonia and suggests that he may have gone there once. The checked Yuhasin also allows that Rav Yehudah may have gone to the Land of Israel. See what I wrote under Rav Hoshaya. How, then, could Rashi write that Rahva was from Pumbedita and we have not found that he went to the Land of Israel? Rav Yehudah was also in Pumbedita, and R' Yehudah Nesia visited him. This is how I thought to defend my ancestor, the gaon Maharshal. But this makes greater the difficulty in Rashi's effort to refute those who explain R' Yehudah as uncertainty between R' Yehudah Ha-Nasi and Rav Yehudah: he was not in R' Yehudah Ha-Nasi's generation and did not see him, but he did see R' Yehudah Nesia, and could have been uncertain whether he heard from Rav Yehudah or R' Yehudah Nesia. Rashi's Pesahim wording is precise: ‘uncertain whether he heard it from Rav Yehudah or R' Yehudah Nesia, who was also in that generation.’ End quotation. If the reading is R' Yehudah Ha-Nasi, he was not in his generation. Still more puzzling is Rashi's objection that Rahva never saw R' Yehudah bar Ilai. How could Rashi think those interpreters did not know R' Yehudah bar Ilai preceded him by much? R' Yehudah Ha-Nasi, namely Rabbi, also preceded him by much. Necessarily those interpreters intended uncertainty between Rav Yehudah and R' Yehudah Nesia, of that generation. Rashi is indeed right that it is impossible to explain ‘Rabbi Yehudah’ by uncertainty about whom he heard: everywhere Rahva says R' Yehudah—in Berakhot, Shabbat, Menahot, the first chapter of Pesahim, quoted above, and the first chapter of Beitzah and Hullin, quoted shortly. How could he be uncertain in all of them? Beitzah 11b: Rahva said that R' Yehudah said: ‘Even one who opens barrels and begins his dough—they permitted its end because of its beginning.’ Rashi explains: ‘R' Yehudah said’: some explain uncertainty whether it was in R' Yehudah Nesia's name or Rav Yehudah's. I say Rahva did not see R' Yehudah Nesia: he was from Pumbedita and we have not found that he went to the Land of Israel. Moreover, when elsewhere they say he learned precisely from his teacher, like Rahva, they should have said he recited even uncertainties about authorities, as in Hullin 18b, where Rav Yosef says Rav Yehudah recited even uncertainties about authorities, such as whether a teaching came from Rav or Shmuel. Heilprin’s quotation gives ‘bar Yehudah.’ In my view he called him Rabbi because he was his principal teacher and he learned from no other, so we would not confuse him with a different Rav Yehudah. End quotation. Tosafot likewise quote Rashi and conclude: the statement that he learned the teaching from his mouth refers to ‘stoa within stoa’: he did not wish to change it to itztavanit, since he heard that wording from his teacher. End quotation; as Rashi writes in Pesahim 52. Hullin 62, end of a: Rahva said that R' Yehudah said, ‘The tasil is unfit,’ etc. Tosafot write: this is the unqualified Rav Yehudah; because he was his principal teacher he said Rabbi Yehudah. Some explain that he was uncertain whether he heard R' Yehudah the tanna or Rav Yehudah the amora, which is why elsewhere it says he learned precisely, like Rahva, etc., who said R' Yehudah said the Temple Mount had a double stoa. This does not appear right: then it should have said he recited even uncertainties about authorities, as with Rav Yehudah above, uncertain whether from Rav, etc. Moreover, when it brings the double-stoa statement, it should also have brought our present teaching. Rather, his precision lay in keeping his teacher's word stoa rather than itztavanit, etc. End quotation. One could defend the interpreters who say it reflects uncertainty about whom he heard, despite its appearing in many places: Yoma 72a has Rahva said that Rav Yehudah said, ‘One who tears priestly garments is flogged’; there, b, Rahva said that Rav Yehudah said, ‘Three arks,’ etc. There he calls him Rav Yehudah. Perhaps in the aforementioned places he was uncertain, so called him R' Yehudah; in the two Yoma places he certainly knew he heard Rav Yehudah, so called him Rav Yehudah. But Rashi's Pesahim explanation of precise learning as uncertainty between Rav Yehudah and R' Yehudah is difficult: how did he not recall that he himself rejected this in Berakhot, since presumably he first wrote his Berakhot commentary? Moreover, there is a contradiction to his Pesahim explanation that precise learning means uncertainties of authorities, from saying R' Yehudah. Why, then, bring it when saying ‘Hold onto Rav Huna, who is precise like Rahva,’ and in Berakhot ‘Hold onto R' Hiyya, who is precise like Rahva, who said R' Yehudah said: double stoa,’ etc.? If the precision were saying Rabbi Yehudah, it should not have said ‘who said stoa,’ etc., only ‘precise like Rahva, who said R' Yehudah said,’ meaning that in all his statements in Rav Yehudah's name he said R' Yehudah. Necessarily ‘precise’ refers to saying stoa rather than itztabba. Later I saw that Tosafot, Berakhot 33, also wrote this and intended this point, which pleased me. Thus the precision is his saying stoa; calling him R' Yehudah is because he was his principal teacher. Consequently Yoma 72a–b should also read Rahva said that R' Yehudah said.

The Arukh, entry רב, writes as follows: ‘Explanation: he was uncertain whether in Rav Yehudah's name or R' Yehudah's, and took care not to interchange teachings, reciting Rabbi. Our master—may he live forever—said: it is not so. Had he said Rabbi, and not said either Rav or Rabbi, it is not a word here, and he gives no reason, and it is no honor to him. Thus he—may he live forever—said: Rahva never saw R' Yehudah; he saw only Rav Yehudah. A scribe erred and wrote R' Yehudah. The geonim of this time saw that there is no Rabbi in that matter, and said thus. These are R' Hananel's words, of blessed memory. For the first explanation we found support in Makom She-Nahagu: Rav Safra said,’ etc. (see above). End quotation. I did not understand his words; perhaps there is some scribal error. I copied it as it stands. Let one whose heart is whole correct it and receive a blessing.

He was Homa’s first husband. She was the daughter of Issi son of Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehudah. Her second husband was Rav Yitzhak son of Rabbah bar bar Hana. After her second husband died, Abaye married her. It is surprising that he was Rav Yehudah's principal pupil yet married his grandson's daughter. Perhaps he was his pupil in Rav Yehudah's old age, or Rahva married Homa in his own old age. His sons were Iffa and Avimi. Heilprin infers that Homa was not their mother because, in his account, both studied Shevuot in Rabbah’s academy (see Shevuot 28b). The checked passage singles out Iffa, spelled Eifa there, as reciting Shevuot and records Avimi questioning him. and R' Yitzhak bar Rav Yehudah, Homa's father's father, also studied Shevuot in Rabbah's academy (see Rav Aha bar Huna). Iffa also questioned Rav Yehudah (see there). He and Rav Huna bar Hinena explained it. He came before Rav Yosef, and Abaye raised an objection (Bava Metzia 29b). He asked Rabbah (Rava in the checked Eruvin 22b); tested the rabbis: there, 76, beginning of a. Rahva said: Shabbat 40b; also at the end of Af Al Pi (Ketubbot 65b). Rahva's sons found difficulty: Shabbat 103, beginning of a.
